name: Neycha Fund
sample_portfolio: Millionstars Health Products (Uganda health supplements, USD 22k/24-month loan, 750 smallholder farmers); indigenous medicinal-herb and food-system entrepreneurs in Uganda and Kenya.
description: Open-ended, evergreen fund (Shona Capital, launched May 2023) advancing regenerative/agroecological food-system entrepreneurs in East Africa via 0%-interest loans and revenue-based financing of USD 10k-50k for working capital and asset financing. Raised USD 960k to date; needs USD 200k in 2025 to sustain growth. Also builds a Community of Practice on Agroecological Entrepreneurship in East Africa. Explicit agroecology mandate.
rationale: V1=4: Agroecology is the fund's reason for existing - a dedicated agroecology accelerator + revolving loan fund (Biovision x SHONA), not a sustainability add-on; applicants are screened with the Business Agroecology Criteria Tool (B-ACT). V2=4: Mandate targets regeneration of soils, biodiversity and circular agrifood systems across the whole value chain (inputs, processing, consumption), and B-ACT scores ecological practice at entry. V3=4: Agroecology defined to include farmer livelihoods and fair, socially just food systems; portfolio reaches smallholders directly (e.g. 750 farmers via Millionstars) and features women founders. V4=3: Producers/AEEs are convened through a Community of Practice on Agroecological Entrepreneurship and B-ACT is applied with them, but selection and credit decisions remain with SHONA Capital - not devolved to producer governance.

name: Agricultural Commodity Transformation Fund ACT Fund
sample_portfolio: Agri-SMEs connecting smallholder farmers to markets across Africa, Latin America and Asia; targets ~275,000 farmers and ~70 investments of USD 1.5-5m each.
description: USD 100m blended-finance vehicle established by the Common Fund for Commodities (UN-affiliated) providing debt financing plus a USD 10m Technical Assistance Facility to agri-SMEs in commodity value chains, explicitly promoting regenerative agriculture, restoring soils/biodiversity/carbon stocks, and de-risking investment. Anchored by a USD 20m CFC first-loss commitment. Explicit regenerative-agriculture orientation ('inclusive regenerative agriculture is at the heart of ACT's transformative investment thesis').
alignment_threshold: Rigorous - regenerative agriculture central to investment thesis
rationale: V1=3: 'Inclusive regenerative agriculture is at the heart of ACT's transformative investment thesis' - an explicit, named commitment to regeneration of soil health alongside community and biodiversity benefits, anchored by USD 20m of CFC first-loss capital. Held at 3 because ACT's own SFDR disclosure states sustainable investment is not its sole objective: it pursues financial return alongside environmental/social characteristics. V2=3: Regenerative practice, soil restoration and biodiversity protection are required focus areas and investees are monitored against defined ESG criteria, but the mechanism is ESG due diligence plus TA on climate-smart outgrower schemes rather than required input elimination and closed cycles. V3=3: Smallholder income and gender inclusion are named, targeted impact areas (SDG 1, 5, 8) with ~275,000 farmers targeted and a USD 10m TA facility; equity is an explicit and monitored criterion, though not rights-based. V4=2: A UN-affiliated, top-down blended vehicle - CFC's Executive Board and the fund's investment committee approve deals; farmers are reached through agri-SME intermediaries and consulted via TA design, with no producer governance role.
regional_breakdown: Sub-Saharan Africa, Latin America, South Asia

name: Alterfin
sample_portfolio: Sustainable-agriculture producer organisations & agri-MFIs across 14 value chains (76% certified organic, 73% fair-trade); ~1m+ smallholders reached.
description: Belgian financial cooperative providing loans (avg ~EUR 336k) and some capacity building to smallholder producer organisations, agri-SMEs and rural MFIs, predominantly in Latin America. Strong organic/fair-trade orientation - watches for sustainable practice over certification - but not an explicit agroecology mandate.
rationale: V1=2: No agroecology mandate. Alterfin lends against organic and fair-trade practice (74-90% of partners certified organic and/or Fairtrade) and says it watches for sustainable practice over certification - that is credible substitution-stage financing of cleaner practice, not a stated goal of system redesign. V2=3: Certification requirements mean ecological criteria are effectively required of partners and tracked through certification audits, covering organic input rules - but the fund does not require diversification, closed cycles or biodiversity outcomes of its own. V3=3 (adjusted from 4): Equity and fair livelihoods are the founding purpose - created by Belgian NGOs and ethical banks to serve those excluded from formal finance, lending to smallholder producer organisations (avg ~EUR 336k, reaching 1m+ smallholders), deliberately targeting the missing middle where it is the first international lender for ~40% of partners, and financing chains where producers receive a price premium. B Corp certified. Not 4, because V3=4 additionally requires gender/marginalised inclusion and rights (land, food, seed) as core measured criteria, and no gender targets or rights-based framing are evidenced. V4=3: A genuine cooperative - ~6,000 member co-owners guide direction through democratic governance, and it lends TO producer organisations and cooperatives. Held at 3 not 4 because the democratic control sits with Belgian investor-members, not with the Southern producers receiving capital.

name: Althelia Climate Fund (Mirova Natural Capital)
sample_portfolio: Peru/Guatemala agroforestry-and-conservation projects producing no-deforestation organic cocoa, coffee and fair-trade beef with carbon revenue.
description: EUR ~100m natural-capital fund (Mirova) investing debt/equity in deforestation-frontier projects combining sustainable agroforestry in buffer zones, forest protection and carbon/REDD+ revenue with fair, sustainable livelihoods. Explicit agroforestry/no-deforestation orientation within a natural-capital thesis.
rationale: V1=3: Explicit agroforestry and no-deforestation orientation on deforestation frontiers, combining buffer-zone agroforestry with forest protection - genuine system framing, but housed inside a natural-capital/carbon investment thesis rather than an agroecology theory of change. V2=4: Portfolio requires no-deforestation organic cocoa and coffee production plus forest conservation, with carbon/REDD+ verification providing external measurement of ecological outcomes. V3=3: Fair and sustainable livelihoods (incl. fair-trade beef and certified organic value chains) are explicit objectives and certification provides tracking, but equity is delivered through certification standards rather than gender/rights criteria set by the fund. V4=2: Capital is deployed as debt/equity into project developers with carbon-revenue structures; communities participate as project partners and beneficiaries, while allocation decisions remain with Mirova Natural Capital's investment committee.

name: Amazon Biodiversity Fund (ABF)
sample_portfolio: Belterra Agroflorestas, Inocas (macauba agroforestry), Amazonia Agroflorestal (coffee agroforestry), Manioca, Horta da Terra - Brazilian Amazon ventures.
description: USD ~50-60m fund (advised by Impact Earth; DFC guarantee) making venture/early-growth equity investments in Brazilian-Amazon enterprises across conservation/reforestation, smallholder value chains, sustainable agriculture and innovation - heavily agroforestry and biodiversity-based. Explicit agroforestry/biodiversity orientation.
rationale: V1=3: Explicit agroforestry and biodiversity thesis for the Brazilian Amazon, and the portfolio is genuinely system-redesign in character (Belterra, Inocas macauba, Amazonia Agroflorestal, Manioca) - but the fund is framed as venture/early-growth equity in Amazon enterprises rather than as an agroecology theory of change referencing HLPE/FAO. V2=4: Agroforestry and biodiversity-based production are the investment screen; conservation and reforestation are explicit outcome categories tracked for investors and the DFC guarantee. V3=3: Smallholder value chains are a named investment pillar and portfolio companies work through farmer networks, so livelihoods are an explicit criterion - but the evidence is enterprise-growth and jobs framing rather than gender/rights targets. V4=3: Investees are Amazon-rooted ventures embedded in local communities and advised by locally-present teams, yet capital allocation sits with the fund adviser and its investment committee - no producer or IPLC governance seats evidenced.

name: EcoEnterprises Fund
sample_portfolio: Kiwa (bio-inputs/agroforestry); nature-based SMEs in regenerative agriculture, agroforestry, sustainable aquaculture and forestry across Latin America.
description: Women-led Latin American impact fund (Fund IV ~USD 150m, GCF-backed) providing mezzanine equity/debt-like growth capital plus advisory to 'missing-middle' nature-based businesses in regenerative agriculture, agroforestry, sustainable forestry and aquaculture. Explicit regenerative-agriculture/agroforestry and biodiversity orientation.
alignment_threshold: Rigorous - regenerative ag & agroforestry central, bio-inputs favoured
rationale: V1=3: Explicit regenerative-agriculture, agroforestry and biodiversity thesis across Fund IV, and it invests in bio-input businesses (Kiwa) - but the framing is nature-based/natural-climate-solutions investing rather than a theory of change built on the HLPE principles, so redesign is emerging rather than the organising logic. V2=4: Investees must protect and restore ecosystems, watersheds and working landscapes; regenerative agriculture, agroforestry, certified forestry and blue economy are the target sectors, and biodiversity outcomes are tracked for GCF reporting. V3=3: A women-led manager with an explicit focus on gender-inclusive and women-led companies, investing in community businesses that collaborate with local peoples, plus a published complaints/grievance channel - equity is a real selection criterion, though not framed around land/seed rights. V4=3: Deep, long-horizon engagement with community enterprises and advisory alongside mezzanine capital, but investment decisions rest with the fund manager; producers are not in fund governance.

name: FINAPOP
sample_portfolio: Cooperana banana-jam cooperative (Nova Uniao, Minas Gerais; USD 24k loan, Dec 2022, 24-month repayment) - production grew from 300,000 to 800,000 units sold 2022-2025. 130 loans totaling USD 14.6m to 64 entities to date.
description: Brazilian cooperative credit fund created by the MST (Landless Workers' Movement, launched 2020) directing resources to family farming, agroecology and grassroots cooperatives for economic, social and environmental return. Raised USD 10.6m to date; 3 investment lines - Productive Investment/CAPEX, Working Capital and Seed Capital. Large unmet pipeline. Explicit agroecology mandate.
rationale: V1=4: Created by the MST (Landless Workers' Movement) explicitly to finance the agroecology transition in agrarian-reform territories - described by FINAPOP as 'the main instrument under land reform to fund organic production and strengthen the agroecology transition'. Agroecology is the political project, not a label. V2=3: Finances organic and agroecological transition among cooperatives with three credit lines (capex, working capital, seed capital); ecological practice is required in substance, but public evidence of portfolio-wide closed-cycle/input-elimination monitoring is thinner than the equity and governance evidence - hence 3 not 4. V3=4: Member family organisations explicitly act on racial justice, gender relations and economic inequalities, run mixed leadership teams and work to keep young people in rural areas; the fund exists to break farmers out of ~48% commercial interest rates, and land rights are the movement's founding cause. V4=4: Grassroots-governed by design - capital is raised from ordinary Brazilian citizens and directed to cooperatives in land-reform settlements, with FINAPOP's project department coordinated from within an MST cooperative board; decisions sit with the movement, not an external manager.
sector_focus: Local markets, some organic exports; food production, seeds & biofertilizers
instrument_detail: 3 credit lines: CAPEX, working capital, seed capital

name: Livelihoods Fund for Family Farming (L3F)
sample_portfolio: Coconut (Philippines), vanilla (Madagascar), shea (Ghana), cocoa and oil-palm smallholder regenerative projects in corporate supply chains.
description: EUR ~120m corporate results-based fund (Danone, Mars, Firmenich, Veolia) financing 10-year landscape/supply-chain projects that shift smallholders to regenerative agriculture and restore ecosystems; recouped by member companies via sustainable sourcing rather than repayment from AEEs. Explicit regenerative-agriculture and ecosystem-restoration focus.
rationale: V1=4: Explicit results-based mandate to shift smallholders to regenerative agriculture and restore ecosystems over 10-year project horizons - transformation, not efficiency, is the contracted deliverable. V2=4: Ecosystem restoration and regenerative practice are the payment triggers (corporates recoup via sustainable sourcing), so ecological outcomes are measured and verified, not optional. V3=3: Smallholder livelihoods in corporate supply chains (coconut, vanilla, shea, cocoa) are explicit project objectives and tracked, but the fund is structured around member-company sourcing interests rather than a rights-based framework. V4=3: Projects are co-designed with producer groups and implemented through local partners over a decade, yet governance sits with the corporate members (Danone, Mars, Firmenich, Veolia) - producers influence design but do not hold fund governance seats.

name: Mirova Land Degradation Neutrality Fund
sample_portfolio: Mountain Hazelnuts (Bhutan), Komaza (Kenya sustainable forestry); 13 sustainable land-use projects across coffee, cocoa, wood, nuts and fresh fruit in Latin America, Africa and Asia.
description: USD ~208m blended-finance debt fund (Mirova, initiated by the UNCCD) investing long-term debt in profit-generating sustainable land-use and land-restoration projects in developing countries - agroforestry, regenerative & sustainable agriculture and sustainable forestry on degraded land, with a junior concessional tranche de-risking senior investors. Explicit land-restoration/agroforestry orientation.
rationale: V1=3: Explicit land-restoration and agroforestry mandate, initiated by the UNCCD to serve Land Degradation Neutrality - a real system-level goal, but expressed as sustainable land use and LDN targets rather than an HLPE-based agroecology theory of change. V2=4: Investments must be profit-generating sustainable land-use projects ON degraded land - restoration, agroforestry and sustainable forestry are the eligibility criteria, with LDN outcomes measured across the 13-project portfolio and a TA facility (LDN TAF) supporting technical standards. V3=3: Smallholder-linked projects (Mountain Hazelnuts, Komaza) and cooperative-transition models are selected partly on livelihood impact and reported on, but the fund lends to project companies against LDN metrics rather than applying rights-based equity criteria. V4=2: Structured as a blended debt fund with a junior concessional tranche de-risking senior private investors; decisions sit with Mirova's investment committee and communities are consulted through project developers - not shaping fund-level allocation.
regional_breakdown: Sub-Saharan Africa, South Asia, Latin America

name: Pachamama
sample_portfolio: COCLA (Cusco, Peru - 8,500+ smallholder indigenous families, <3 hectares each; ~160,000 lbs certified-organic coffee purchased in 2025 for ~USD 800k, ~200,000 lbs/USD 1m expected 2026). Roasts and sells USD 8m annually to 10,000+ customers.
description: Farmer-owned, vertically-integrated coffee cooperative and roaster (launched 2006, 5 countries) 100% created, owned and governed by its member farmer cooperatives, selling roasted coffee directly to end-consumers so farmers earn ~7x more than Fair Trade coffee farmers (capturing ~USD 18/lb vs USD 2.40 for Fair Trade). Self-raised USD 381k in equity retaining 100% ownership; seeking USD 2m in financing for green (raw) coffee purchases in 2026. Explicit regenerative-organic farming orientation.
alignment_threshold: Rigorous - regenerative organic farming central to farmer-ownership model
rationale: V1=4: A farmer-owned cooperative and roaster built to restructure who captures value in coffee - regenerative-organic production is tied directly to farmer ownership of the downstream business, which is system redesign rather than practice substitution. V2=4: Certified-organic regenerative production is the operating standard across member cooperatives (e.g. ~160,000 lbs certified-organic coffee purchased from COCLA in 2025), so input elimination and soil practice are built into the supply base, not encouraged. V3=4: The entire value proposition is fair livelihoods - farmers capture ~USD 18/lb versus ~USD 2.40 for Fair Trade coffee, roughly 7x Fair Trade farmer earnings, across 8,500+ smallholder indigenous families farming under 3 hectares each. V4=4: 100% created, owned and governed by its member farmer cooperatives, and it self-raised USD 381k of equity while retaining full farmer ownership - producer governance is the legal structure, the strongest possible V4 evidence.
instrument_detail: Cooperative equity / self-financed; seeking green-coffee purchase finance

name: Shared Interest Society
sample_portfolio: Fairtrade coffee, cocoa, nut and handcraft producer organisations and buyers across Africa, Latin America and Asia.
description: UK ethical-finance cooperative providing trade credit, export finance and term loans to Fairtrade-certified producer organisations and fair-trade buyers. Fair-trade/sustainable-livelihoods orientation; agroecology practices incidental rather than an explicit mandate.
rationale: V1=2: Fair-trade finance, not agroecology. The mandate is trade credit and export finance for Fairtrade-certified producer organisations; agroecological practice arrives via certification standards rather than as a stated transformation goal. V2=3: Fairtrade certification imposes required environmental standards (restricted materials lists, some organic conversion) that are externally audited, so ecological criteria are required and tracked - but the fund sets no input-elimination, diversification or biodiversity requirements itself. V3=3 (adjusted from 4): Fair trade justice IS the mandate - a UK ethical-finance cooperative providing the working capital that lets certified producer organisations get paid promptly and trade on fair terms; fair prices and decent livelihoods are the reason the lender exists and are verified through Fairtrade certification. Not 4, because no gender/marginalised inclusion targets or land/seed rights criteria are evidenced as fund criteria. V4=3: Member-owned ethical cooperative lending directly to producer organisations (which are themselves democratically farmer-governed), so producers hold real power at the borrower level - but Shared Interest's own governance is held by UK investor-members, not Southern producers.
regional_breakdown: Sub-Saharan Africa, Latin America, South Asia

name: SIDI
sample_portfolio: KOPAKAMA (Rwanda coffee cooperative), Nyesigiso (Mali), SIPEM Banque (Madagascar); 100+ agri-food SMEs, producer organisations, cooperatives and microfinance institutions across ~36 countries, mostly Africa and Latin America.
description: French solidarity social investor (created 1983 by CCFD-Terre Solidaire) providing loans, equity participations, guarantees and technical assistance to agri-food SMEs, producer organisations, cooperatives and MFIs in developing countries, mostly Africa and Latin America. Since 2017 has placed the Ecological and Social Transition - including agroecology - at the centre of its strategy. Explicit agroecology orientation within a solidarity-finance mandate.
rationale: GATE: set to Pass by iGravity. Note the desk evidence is a positive agroecological analysis grid, not an exclusion list - confirm the exclusion scope at Tier 2. V1=3: Agroecology is named strategy, not branding. SIDI placed the ecological and social transition at the centre of its 2017-21 strategic plan, created an internal agroecology working group in 2018, adopted a formal AGROECOLOGICAL ANALYSIS GRID to assess and question partners' practices and support their transition, and trained partnership officers on applying it across priority value chains (cocoa, coffee, market gardening, rice, maize). Redesign is emerging and institutionalised - held below 4 only because agroecology sits within a broader solidarity-finance mandate rather than driving all allocation. V2=3: The grid makes ecological practice an explicit, assessed criterion, and SIDI actively supports green fertilisers, agroforestry, solar irrigation and biomass/by-product valorisation upstream with partners. Not 4: the grid guides transition rather than requiring input elimination or closed cycles, and there is no portfolio-wide ecological monitoring evidenced. V3=3: Founded by CCFD-Terre Solidaire in 1983 explicitly to improve conditions for vulnerable and MARGINALISED populations excluded from economic circuits, investing deliberately in fragile and 'at-risk' rural zones others avoid; gender equality (egalite femmes-hommes) features in its impact reporting. Equity is explicit and tracked, but not framed around land/food/seed rights. V4=3: Unusually strong for a Northern investor - SIDI takes equity stakes specifically to obtain BOARD SEATS at partner organisations (e.g. 23% / EUR 130k securing two director posts) and accompanies partners on governance itself; partners are largely peasant/producer organisations and cooperatives pursuing autonomy, and SIDI's own capital comes from ~2,000 activist shareholders and 3,500 solidarity savers. Not 4: SIDI's own decisions are made by SIDI-Gestion SAS (CCFD-Terre Solidaire plus three religious congregations) via the comite de gerance; producers influence at partner level, not in SIDI's governance.

name: The Lirio Fund
sample_portfolio: Kulkao (Huanuco, Peru - organic cacao processing, 400+ smallholder farmers, 50+ jobs at organic-certified plant, exports to Europe/North America). 31 loans completed with 23 companies; 98% repayment rate.
description: NESsT-managed debt fund (launched ~2018, 28-year NESsT track record) providing debt and mezzanine capital to high-impact social enterprises in the 'missing middle' (USD 50k-500k) creating dignified jobs for rural, at-risk communities in the Andes and Amazon. Raised USD 12.8m (USD 10.7m senior debt, USD 1.4m subordinated debt, USD 450k equity); targeting USD 15m AUM by 2025 and USD 50m by 2030 (every USD 1 of sub-debt raises USD 5 of senior debt). Explicit conservation and organic-farming orientation.
alignment_threshold: Moderate - conservation and organic-farming practice screen
rationale: GATE: set to Pass by iGravity. Note the desk evidence is a stated PREFERENCE for organic/Fair Trade/Rainforest Alliance standards rather than a binding exclusion list - confirm at Tier 2 whether certification is required. V1=2: Agroecology is not the thesis. Lirio is a livelihoods-and-conservation fund - its stated purpose is dignified formal jobs for marginalised communities in the Andes-Amazon plus sustainable land management, and its 2023 repositioning was toward livelihoods and land management, not agroecological redesign. Ecological practice arrives via certification preference, i.e. substitution stage. V2=3: Ecological criteria are real and applied at selection - preference for organic, Fair Trade or Rainforest Alliance certification (organic certification excludes GMOs and most synthetics at investee level, e.g. Kulkao's organic-certified cacao plant), plus a deep conservation focus on deforestation-free supply chains and enterprises actively protecting or restoring landscapes. Not 4: certification preference is not input elimination or closed cycles, and it is a preference rather than a portfolio-wide requirement. V3=4: This is the fund's core, and it is measured. Explicit selection criterion that a loan must create at least 50 jobs for marginalised communities; deliberate emphasis on women, indigenous-led ventures and marginalised groups (smallholder farmers, youth, Indigenous peoples); portfolio supports 2,400+ smallholders and vulnerable workers of whom 45% are women; targets formalising employment and raising incomes 25-50%; portfolio enterprises promote gender equity and hold strong relationships with indigenous communities, including enterprises drawing on generations of traditional rainforest knowledge. Dignified livelihoods and marginalised-group inclusion are core, tracked criteria. V4=2: The weak axis. Enterprises maintain strong community and indigenous relationships and some are indigenous-led, but Lirio is a NESsT-managed debt fund - credit decisions sit with NESsT's investment team and CIO. Communities are consulted and employed rather than shaping allocation; no participatory grantmaking or producer governance seats evidenced.
sector_focus: Local & export; rural social enterprises (cacao, coffee, cotton)
investee_profile: Missing-middle' high-impact social enterprises creating dignified rural jobs

name: The Moringa Fund
sample_portfolio: Portfolio of ~10 agroforestry projects incl. sustainable heart-of-palm (Brazil), coconut/lime on degraded land (Belize), certified coffee & timber (Nicaragua).
description: EUR 84-100m private-equity fund (Edmond de Rothschild / ONF International) financing profitable large-scale agroforestry in Sub-Saharan Africa and Latin America via EUR 4-10m equity/quasi-equity tickets, plus the ATAF technical-assistance facility. Explicit agroforestry orientation (a core agroecology archetype).
alignment_threshold: Rigorous - agroforestry is the investment thesis
rationale: V1=3: Agroforestry IS the investment thesis (the manager describes itself as financing the agro-ecology transition) and it leverages the inherent sustainability of agroforestry to distinguish itself from other land-based strategies - but the model is large-scale, profit-first plantation agroforestry, so redesign is emerging rather than the whole allocation logic. V2=3 (adjusted from 4): Every investment must combine trees with crops or livestock (silvoarable/silvopastoral), generating soil-fertility, erosion and water-quality benefits, and the ONFI-run ATAF facility develops and monitors the models technically - so ecological criteria are required and tracked. Not 4, because there is no input-elimination or closed-cycle requirement: the ATAF programme itself procures agricultural inputs, seeds and seedlings. V3=2: Social impact is expressed as jobs and outgrower income (targets of ~8,000 jobs and ~60,000 outgrowers; ~10,500 smallholders reached as suppliers), with ESG risk analysis suggested by ONFI - inclusion language is present and partially tracked, but there are no gender or rights-based selection criteria, and smallholders are suppliers to an industrial nucleus rather than rights-holders. V4=2: Moringa takes minority participations in project companies via shareholder agreements and works with private project promoters; participatory methods appear only in TA research design. Communities are consulted around projects but do not shape capital allocation.

name: Urapi Sustainable Land Use Fund (Ecotierra)
sample_portfolio: Cafe Selva Norte (Peru coffee agroforestry + carbon); community agroforestry cooperatives in coffee, cocoa, nuts and timber across Latin America.
description: USD ~51m fund (managed by Ecotierra Capital) providing long-term debt and equity plus embedded TA and carbon finance to community-based regenerative agroforestry projects that renovate farms, restore degraded land and conserve forests in Latin America. Explicit regenerative-agroforestry orientation.
rationale: V1=4: The whole vehicle exists to move cooperatives off degrading land-use into regenerative agroforestry - Ecotierra grew out of 20+ years of cooperative work (originally the non-profit Pro-A) and frames its model as co-creation letting producers control their own economic, social and environmental growth. V2=4: Agroforestry systems are implemented to improve soil health and biodiversity, with input substitution taken to production scale - the RioSierra project set up Granja BioAgricola to make and distribute bio-fertiliser, displacing synthetic fertiliser regionally; monitored via MINKA plus Verra/Organic/Fairtrade verification. V3=4: Explicit goal of tripling partner-cooperative household incomes, Fairtrade/organic certification, and processing infrastructure (dry mill, collection centres, compost plant) CO-OWNED by the cooperatives - i.e. value and assets transfer to producers, not just price premiums. V4=4: Projects are co-designed with cooperatives over multi-year processes (RioSierra approved after ~3 years of co-design and consultation with Red Ecolsierra), producers co-own the assets, and independent governance oversees the fund.

name: Aavishkaar Capital
sample_portfolio: Agriculture value-chain, financial-inclusion and essential-services enterprises across India, South/Southeast Asia and Africa.
description: Emerging-markets impact venture-capital manager providing equity to enterprises across agriculture value chains, financial inclusion and essential services. Inclusive-development framing; agriculture is a core sector but not an explicit agroecology mandate.

name: Barka Fund
sample_portfolio: AFREX Gold (Kenya avocado exporter, est. 2005, aggregates fruit from 1,200 smallholder farmers; 2025 investment of USD 300k equity + USD 300k loan expected to plant 50,000 trees and raise local incomes 30%, growing margins 22% to 31% over 5 years).
description: African-led fund (launched 2024, backed by Barka Impact Foundation) investing in African climate companies with high growth potential, partnering with management teams to scale and achieve positive financial returns alongside environmental, social and development benefits; focus on aggregator companies benefiting smallholder farmers. USD 11m fund (USD 4m equity, USD 7m debt), targeting USD 20m fund size and seeking USD 9m in additional equity. Climate/restoration framing; not an explicit agroecology mandate.
rationale: V1=2: Agroecology is not the thesis. Barka is an early-stage African climate venture fund (launched 2020, first-time manager) investing across three sectors - environment & natural resources, agriculture & food systems, and energy - with agriculture priorities stated as 'enhancing agricultural productivity, reducing food loss and optimizing input and system efficiency'. That is efficiency/substitution framing, not system redesign, and roughly one-third of the fund is earmarked for restoration alongside sustainable agriculture and renewable energy. No reference to HLPE/FAO agroecology principles. V2=2: Ecological ambition is real but framed as land restoration and carbon, not agroecological practice: climate impact targets align with AFR100 (100m ha restored by 2030) and the Great Green Wall, and portfolio companies do practise agroforestry-type production (Herou Alliance supplies farmers with climate-smart seeds and organic fertilizers to plant moringa alongside existing trees and crops; AFREX Gold's 2025 investment is expected to plant 50,000 trees). Held at 2 because ecological practice is encouraged at investee level rather than a required, monitored portfolio-wide criterion, and 'input efficiency' is not input reduction or closed cycles. V3=3: Equity is explicit and tracked. SDG 5 (gender equality) is one of only two core SDGs alongside SDG 13, the fund is African-women-led, at least 40% of Barka programme participants are women-led, and its gender-inclusive investment approach includes gender analysis of investee value chains, quotas in the TA programme and dedicated coaching/mentoring; smallholder farmers (mostly women and youth) are the stated end beneficiaries. Not 4: equity is delivered through gender targets and jobs/income framing rather than land, food or seed rights criteria. V4=2: Centralised allocation. Barka works exclusively through incubators and accelerators to screen applicants, runs an investment-readiness programme and then makes equity/debt decisions with its own team; smallholders are reached indirectly as suppliers to aggregator companies (e.g. AFREX Gold's 1,200 farmers) and restoration is 'presented as a business case' built into loan terms. Producers are consulted and benefit but do not shape selection or hold fund governance roles; no participatory or devolved decision-making evidenced. TOTAL 9/16 - Medium alignment: credible restoration and gender substance, but agroecology-adjacent rather than agroecology-led. Tier 1 desk assessment; confirm at Tier 2 whether any binding ecological exclusion list applies at investee level.

V4=1: Consultation is project-level and time-bound - &Green worked with local stakeholders over ~12 months to build one ESAP/LPP. V1=2: This is a capital-markets refinancing instrument, not an agroecology vehicle. A USD 450m use-of-proceeds green bond carrying ICMA's Nature Bond secondary designation, ring-fenced to three eligible lending categories (Sustainable Primary Production, Sustainable Agri-Processing, Water Supply & Sanitation). The goal is nature-positive commercial lending at scale; agroecology is not referenced and Column H is 'Generic'. Note the bond also refinanced USD 350m of existing 8.75% notes - a treasury function alongside the impact one. V2=3: Genuinely stronger than typical bank green bonds and the reason this is not a 2. Every eligible loan carries SEVEN independently verified sustainability conditions, with deforestation screening and supply-chain traceability built in; Moody's assigned its highest sustainability quality score (SQS1 Excellent); and 81% of the eligible lending pool is directed at countries where agricultural land-use change is the primary driver of biodiversity loss. Ecological criteria are therefore required and independently monitored. Not 4: the conditions target deforestation, traceability and freshwater protection - not input reduction, diversification, closed cycles or on-farm synergy. V3=2: Smallholder farmers are the stated first beneficiary category and Ecobank frames the bond around 'the farmers, cooperatives and communities whose livelihoods depend on healthy ecosystems', but livelihood benefit is asserted as an outcome of lending rather than set as a measured selection criterion. This is a commercial bank balance-sheet instrument: bondholders on the LSE provide capital, Ecobank's credit and sustainability functions set eligibility, and farmers are end-borrowers screened against conditions written in Lome and verified by third parties. Producers and IPLCs have no role in eligibility design, allocation or verification. Rachael Antwi's remark that nature finance 'has too often been discussed far from the communities it is meant to support' is an argument for proximity of capital, not for devolved decision-making.
